To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the response of healing cornea to a synthetic polymer surface with parallel grooves depends on groove depth.

1) the migration of corneal epithelial cells in vitro and in vivo is directed by the geometry of grooves in a silicone polymer, 2) the direction of epithelial cell migration is towards the deepest point in the groove and 3) the rate of migration is reduced by the presence of grooves.
the nature and rate of corneal epithelial migration over a polymer surface is dependent on the geometry of surface features.

the use of a wound healing process to incorporate a polymer lens into the cornea and the influence of topographical cues on the epithelium.
understanding and controlling the response of healing epithelium to a synthetic polymer lens to facilitate its integration into cornea and the use of this technology to improve the quality of vision.
understanding how the corneal epithelial wound heals and how it can be manipulated to facilitate the incorporation of an implantable contact lens.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
parallel grooves are not optimal to guide epithelial migration.
the response of healing corneas to grooved polymer implants was complex and that the effect of surface geometry on tissue migration was dependent on both the pitch and depth of the grooves.
the response of the healing corneal tissue was highly dependent on the geometry and depth of the grooves.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a flat polymer surface is the best surface for epithelial tissue migration.

the epithelial response to topography is highly dependent on groove depth.
